extracted.intended_audience: math contest students and problem-solvers (Olympiad training / advanced high-school and undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of problem-solving heuristics and techniques (with short examples/hints) for solving integer-function and combinatorial problems from an Olympiad-style problem set; intended to guide solving and constructing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting (count in two ways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the same combinatorial quantity by two different methods and equate them to derive a contradiction or identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: color regions/triangles and count boundary edges from blue-triangle perspective (each counted once → 3b) and from red-country perspective (3r+5), get 3b = 3r+5 contradiction. Widely applicable to combinatorial geometry and graph problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcounting with symmetry correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Count constructions by choices that overcount equivalent objects, then divide by the symmetry factor to get the correct count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: triangulations of an n-gon counted by choosing a vertex and a sequence of diagonals (n·2^{n-4}) then noting each triangulation counted twice → final n·2^{n-5}. Typical for counting structures where labeling/choice causes multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model relations as graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate people/knowing relations or movement constraints into graph vertices and edges, then apply graph-theoretic counting/argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: persons as vertices and acquaintances as edges; use graph properties (degrees, cycles) to deduce contradictions (count cycles through a vertex). Useful to convert social/interaction problems into combinatorial graph problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle / Dirichlet principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition possibilities into boxes and force two objects into the same box to deduce existence statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with 1018 numbers in an interval partitioned into 1017 subintervals, two must fall in the same subinterval → their difference has desired smallness. Also used to force at least 3 edges of same color among 5 incident edges (monochromatic triangle argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive counterexample / extremal coloring
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibit an explicit coloring or construction to show a bound is sharp (or that a certain property need not hold below a threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show 32-edge coloring without monochromatic triangle (diagram Fig. 14.5) proving n=33 is minimal. When proving minimality, give explicit construction for lower values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite descent / infinite descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a minimal counterexample exists and derive a smaller one repeatedly to obtain contradiction; or repeatedly reduce parameters to force equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used multiple times: to show smallest square in a partition cannot touch boundary (otherwise produce smaller one), to reduce integral weights by halving to eventually force equality. A standard number-theoretic/Diophantine technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backwards / inversion (Jacobi's dictum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of building forwards, suppose the target is attainable and deduce previous states uniquely — often simplifies state-space or reveals invariants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: binary-circle transformations (011101000 → ...), removing weights by thinking of process in reverse to generate removals; water-pouring problem solved by tracing backwards denominators. When invariance is not evident, try reverse construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and modular reduction (especially mod 2^k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze parities and higher 2-adic valuations; reduce by factors of 2 (or other primes) repeatedly to deduce stronger constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: weights balancing property implies all weights have same parity; divide by 2 repeatedly to show all weights equal. Many problems use parity counting of lists or congruences mod powers of primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange/averaging / swapping argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Model repeated swaps/exchanges and count total traversals or exchanges to deduce existence of a long/short path or particular property by averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: place a hiker at each vertex and swap along segments from shortest to longest; since each segment traversed twice, total traversed = 2r gives at least one hiker traversed ≥2r/n segments, implying existence of increasing-length path of given length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal principle (choose largest/smallest element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on a maximal or minimal element to obtain inequalities or structure; often leads to uniqueness or alternation patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choose the smallest square in a tiling to get contradiction; in sequence problems pick the largest element to deduce alternation 1 and 0 or equality of all solutions. A standard extremal-method tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity counting of adjacency lists (odd/even combinatorial lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count entries in adjacency or friend-lists and use parity to deduce evenness/oddness of degrees and derive contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (problem 10): for each person A let M be set of friends; sum entries in lists is even since equals twice number of pairs, but each list has odd size → contradiction used to show existence of two persons with even number of common friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity via pigeonhole on finite-state sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the finiteness of states (e.g., 10^4 quadruples) to force repetition and deduce periodicity of sequences extendable uniquely both directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: extending digit sequences and argue there are only 10^4 quadruples so repetition implies a period; unique extensibility yields pure period and later appearance of certain quadruple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominator form powers of two in pouring problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When pouring operations halve quantities, track denominators backward to show initial amounts must have denominators 2^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: water-pouring backward analysis shows denominators of amounts are of form 2^k, hence initial n must be divisible by a power of 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conjugates / algebraic conjugation to prove rationality/integrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider conjugates of algebraic numbers, square/simplify expressions, and use symmetry to force rationality or integer relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: to show certain combinations are rational, square and manipulate using conjugates; to show algebraic integers satisfy integer polynomials one may need two squarings. Many exercises use conjugation to eliminate radicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution and duplication: x = 4 sin^2 alpha
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace algebraic iterates by trigonometric expressions to exploit duplication/angle-doubling identities and make iteration explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: iteration f(x) maps x0=4 sin^2 α to x1=4 sin^2 2α, x2=4 sin^2 4α, giving xn=4 sin^2 2^n α and simplifying analysis of orbits for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent Möbius transformations by complex numbers / multiply representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Map fractional linear transformations (ax+b)/(−bx+a) to rotations / complex numbers; composition becomes multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: associate f(x) to complex number e^{−π i/6}; then g corresponds to z^{1994}; compute power of complex number to get resulting Möbius transform explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve trig-functional equations via angle arguments (roots via sin/cos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert algebraic trig identities into angle equations (sin kt or cos kt equals something), find t from linear equations in angles then recover x=cos t etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transform polynomial/trig identities into sin 8t − sin t = 0 leading to 7t = 2πk or 9t = π + 2πk hence get cos values; other problems use cos 3t identities and half-angle manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity arguments to ensure uniqueness of solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use monotonicity of functions like x^x to argue number of solutions or uniqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show xx is strictly increasing for x>1 to deduce uniqueness in equation comparisons; monotonicity arguments can produce single-solution claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift-invariance / translational argument for functional equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use how expressions change under adding a fixed increment to deduce equality for all x by considering shifts (often by 1/n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if increasing x by 1/n permutes terms on left and increases right by 1, deduce equality holds for any x by tracking how both sides change under shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice-point counting via floor sums (reciprocity counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count lattice points under a diagonal in two ways — directly by area formula and by summing floor(kq/p) to equate and derive identities involving gcd conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: number of integer lattice points with 1 ≤ x ≤ q−1, 1 ≤ y ≤ p−1 below diagonal OB equals (p−1)(q−1)/2 and also sum_{k=1}^{q−1} floor(kp/q), giving classical reciprocity/counting identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box principle for small differences / decimal approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition an interval into many small subintervals and apply pigeonhole to guarantee two numbers are close enough; use to construct small fractional differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set S of 10^18 numbers in [0,d) partitioned into 10^18−1 intervals ⇒ two numbers in same interval give difference less than desired threshold (used to get r+s·3^{-1} small).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary expansion argument to force contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Express real numbers in binary expansion, choose n depending on highest indices to force inequalities or contradictions via binary truncation choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: write a and b as sums of 2^{-a_i}, choose n = 2^{b_t} − 1 to compare (a+b)^n with a^n + b^n and conclude only one of a,b can be nonzero under given inequality constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence relation analysis for divisibility and valuation propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze linear recurrences to deduce divisibility patterns of terms (2-adic valuation growth/shrinkage) and propagate parity/divisibility across indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sequences an obeying an+2 = 6an+1 + 2an give integer/divisibility constraints; show that if an is even/odd then subsequent terms change parity in predictable way, proving divisibility claims by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric circle interpretation of fractional parts / symbolic sequence constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: View fractional parts an+b mod 1 on unit circle and map to binary sequences (upper half → 0, lower half → 1) to analyze which binary words can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: many zeros in a row implies |a| small; subword 010 requires |a|>1/4, contradiction shows that for k≥5 certain binary words (00010) cannot occur; use circle geometry for combinatorial constraints on symbolic sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use similarity and sine law to translate linear conditions into trig expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct geometric figures (triangles) where segment sums correspond to sines of angles; use similarity and Sine Law to obtain explicit formulas for sequences in terms of trig functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: take chain of segments |A0A1|,...,|A9A10| and build isosceles triangle to show angles divided into equal α (15°) and express x1..x5 via sin(kα)/sin((k+1)α) formulas leading to explicit values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding algebraic quantities via products of conjugates and invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Form integer products of conjugate algebraic expressions invariant under field automorphisms to bound individual factors away from zero and derive size estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show product P of four conjugates a ± b·3^{1/2} is integer and |P|≥1, deduce |Fi| ≥ 1/|other_factors| > small epsilon, useful to obtain explicit lower bounds for algebraic numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry + extremal argument to force equal variables in cyclic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cyclic symmetry and choosing an extremal element (largest/smallest) to derive contradictions unless all variables are equal (or alternate), forcing particular discrete solution patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a cyclic system of inequalities, pick largest x1 then deduce chain of inequalities leading to u=v and by symmetry all variables equal or alternate ±1/3 solutions; standard for symmetric cyclic systems.
